Messages.Author: echia...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
At the two most recent U.S. qualifiers, I have noticed a handful of
irregularities that I feel necessitate some discussion and analysis.
Please note that I bring up these issues *not* for the purpose of
whining or complaining. Instead I think the issues warrant some
discussion so that these problems can be avoided in future tournaments
and qualifiers.

#1. At the 2005 East Central Qualifier in Northfield, New Jersey the
event was initially advertised as having a 2.5 hour time limit. However
midway through the tournament the time limit was changed - the first
two rounds had a time limit of 2.5 hours but the third round and the
final had a time limit of 2 hours. After the first round, I had heard
some talk about changing the time limits for the remaining rounds but
since the second round still had a 2.5 time limit, I thought the notion
had been dismissed. Prior to the third round I was not aware that the
time limits had changed. Perhaps other individuals heard such an
announcement or maybe I had stepped away during that moment, but I did
not hear any such announcement. I only learned that the time limit had
changed midway through the game when there was only one hour left. At
that point I immediately began to take a more aggressive position in
the game because I knew that time would be an issue. Although I tried
to emphasize to the other players to play quickly, on at least one
occasion I was rebuffed with the response that the player had the right
to take his time with his turn.

The frustrating thing is that if the second round had been shorter (2
hours instead of 2.5 hours) then that would have resulted in a game win
for me. Alternatively, if the third round had been longer (2.5 hours
instead of 2 hours) then I also would have had a game win for me. I
think the change in time limits was highly irregular and can't help
but feel that I was screwed by it.

Now I am aware that the tournament started late and there was some
concern about the weather. However, having flown into D.C. from Chicago
and carpooled from D.C. to Northfield, I will say that the weather
wasn't really that bad at all.

In addition, I believe that having a game win (if the second round had
been shorter or the third round had been longer) would have made a
significant difference. I ended up placing 6th place. Ben Peal was in
the finals but was already qualified, meaning that the next top four
players would qualify (thus I was right at the brink of qualification).
Truth be told, it's not that big of an issue to me anymore since I
qualified in Boston, though perhaps whoever placed 9th in Boston might
want to put a word or two in (e.g. if I had qualified in New Jersey,
then the 9th place person would have qualified in Boston).

Even if there is nothing in the tournament rules against changing time
limits in the middle of a tournament, it does seem abnormal. In
addition, this also opens the door to potential abuse. For example, one
could advertise the event as having a 2 hour time limit but then in the
middle of the tournament, change the time limit to 1000 hours. This
would then in turn give the locals a major home advantage (they
wouldn't have long drive times or have to worry about catching
flights). Granted that's an extreme corner-case scenario but still.
Also, changing time limits midway may improperly favor some deck
archetypes over others. If I choose a slower-building wall deck on the
knowledge that there's a sizable time limit, I'll definitely get
screwed if the time limit is abruptly shortened.

#2. At the 2005 Northeast Qualifier in Mansfield, Massachusetts, there
was initially a problem because a handful of players had included
reprinted cards from the Kindred Most Wanted expansion in their decks
(the cards were reprints from the starters but the problem is that none
of the Kindred Most Wanted cards, even reprinted ones, were legal yet).
Initially the tournament organizer announced the situation to all of
the participants and said that if anyone had a problem, to speak up. No
one spoke up. Scott Gomes and I were a little concerned about it and we
spoke to the tournament organizer to get some more details, like what
particular cards were at issue. I personally wanted to make sure the
cards weren't hard-to-get rares like Call the Great Beast, Alastor,
Mylan Horseed, etc. When it turned out to be mainly commons and
uncommons, Scott and I suggested that to avoid any sense of
impropriety, it might be easier to just find legal copies of those
cards and sub them in. Fortunately Scott happened to have legal copies
of most of those cards so the situation was quickly rectified.

The lesson from this experience is to please please please understand
what cards are tournament legal and which ones are not (especially in
regards to new expansions and sets). This is something that both
players and organizers should be well aware of prior to playing in a
tournament. Another minor issue is that it is my understanding that
there were actually a handful of other individuals who were
uncomfortable about the situation. However the requirement to speak out
if they had a problem, in such an open forum, would make them feel
awkward. Instead they should be permitted to lodge a complaint in
private, if necessary.

#3. At the 2005 Northeast Qualifier in Mansfield, Massachusetts, there
was one other irregularity that I was concerned about. Now I did not
witness this event directly and this is only my second-hand account of
what happened. Those who were involved in the situation should feel
free to provide elaboration and/or corrections:

The game is down to: Player A --> Player B --> Player C

It is Player B's turn. Player C has 1 pool left and 2 Anarch Revolts
in play, so Player B is not going to bother bleeding C out, since the
Anarch Revolts will kill him next turn. Player B has Le Dinh Tho and
some Shambling Hordes out and is deciding if he wants to do anything
else. Since Player C believes he is dead, he begins to gather up all
his cards and pack up (putting his hand into his library, taking all of
his vampires in torpor and from the ready region).

The problem is that Player A has a Life Boon in hand and was planning
to play it when Player C was going to die. Since Player C had a lot of
minions (some in torpor, some not), and was preemptively packing up,
Player A felt that it would be impossible to reconstruct the game state
if he did not stop Player C. Player A told Player C to not pack up and
that he had a way to save him. In response, Player B used Le Dinh Tho
to make Player A discard his Life Boon.

Thus because Player C improperly packed up his cards before he was
actually ousted, Player A was forced to reveal his hand and was
unfairly penalized as a result.

* Please also note that Player A was playing an Anson Anarch Revolt
deck, so a Life Boon wasn't completely out of left field.

Now I understand that this is a difficult situation. If it were to
happen again, this is what I would suggest: Player A does not say
anything about having a way to save Player C, and simply allows Player
C to pack up. When Player B ends his turn, and the Anarch Revolts would
oust Player C, Player A plays the Life Boon. Reconstruct the game state
as best as possible but if the previous game state could not be fully
established then just let Player C sit there as a pool buffer. Since
Player C had already given up, treat him as if he were not going to
bother taking any actions or blocking.

This was significant because Player B was close to being ousted and if
Player C had not prematurely packed up, then there is a good chance
that Player A would have gotten a game win. This would have meant that
Player A would have qualified and that he/she would have made the
finals as well.

The lesson from this experience is please please please don't
completely pack up unless you are actually ousted. Or if you really do
want to give up and pack up, be okay with "doing nothing" during
your turn if you miraculously do survive.

#4. During the Starter/Draft event following the Northeast Qualifier, I
am not sure if sufficient time was given for deck construction. Now
please note that I *was* on time for the event (surprise, surprise). I
was playing the Alastors deck and I didn't make many changes (took
out 3 library cards and 1 crypt card, added a dozen library cards and 3
or 4 crypt cards) so I *know* I did not spend a lot of time actually
constructing my deck. Instead, I knew that I would have to spend most
of the deck construction time sleeving my deck instead. Now some of my
fellow players *strongly* expressed their dissatisfaction regarding the
time I was taking to sleeve my deck. I feel that I was unfairly singled
out. Yes, I did need some time to fully prepare my deck. On the other
hand however, I am an extremely fast and efficient drafter. Having
previously played in two KMW pre-releases, I was already fairly
familiar with most of the cards we were drafting. There were some
individuals however who were taking a great deal of time reading every
single new card. Now I certainly am not begrudging these individuals
for taking the time to read the cards. But I don't think it's right
that I got all the flak for taking too much time sleeving my cards when
other individuals took just as much time, if not more, reading cards
and drafting.

Once again I want to emphasize that the purpose of this post was not to
bitch and moan. I had a great time at both qualifier events and want to
applaud all of the organizers for a job well done. There's always
room for improvement however, so by bringing some of these issues to
the forefront, I'm hoping we can all have a constructive
conversation.

With regards,
- Eric Chiang

There's two issues here. One is just the concept of changing the time
limit at all. In this case, the change was modest but it still makes
a difference. People could build decks that are even sensative to the
difference between a two hour and a two-and-a-half hour time limit. I
think there's a lot of tournament organizers out there who are annoyingly
oblivious to what effects their "minor changes" have on players. I'd
say such organizers should be slapped a couple of times to get their
attention except they're usually volunteers donativing their time for the
common good and who often have a lot of other shit to worry about.

Changing the time limit of a round without making sure all the players
are aware of it AT THE START OF THE GAME is really bad, though! That
could cost someone big time - either a qualifying shot or a chance at
the finals. Hopefully, this will get corrected somehow. (By "corrected",
I mean the organizer being made aware that this happened and it isn't an
acceptable way to run a sanctioned tournament, let alone a qualifier).

> #2. At the 2005 Northeast Qualifier in Mansfield, Massachusetts, there
> was initially a problem because a handful of players had included

> (the cards were reprints from the starters but the problem is that none

> Initially the tournament organizer announced the situation to all of

You're not clear about this. You mean, they indended to _allow_ this?
The organizers have to know the rules about legal decks. I have no
problem with taking a little extra time and allowing players to make
their decks legal, however they need to do it (including finding legal
copies of illegal cards). But they shouldn't be expecting other players
to tolerate illegal decks, even if by virtue of reprinted not-yet-legal
cards. (Yea, I know it's kind of a funky rule and I personally don't
agree with it. But rules are rules and it does make a difference.)



> The lesson from this experience is please please please don't
> completely pack up unless you are actually ousted. Or if you really do
> want to give up and pack up, be okay with "doing nothing" during
> your turn if you miraculously do survive.

This one is a lot nittier. I have trouble blaming either player C
or a judge (for not stopping player C). Yea, you're right, people
should toe the line and not behave like they're ousted until they're
physically ousted - but it's such a corner-case situation that (even
with the Anarch Revolt deck - many AR decks don't bother with Life
Boon) that I have to write this down to being kind of off-the-wall.
Say, there's five Anarch Revolts out and player C has five pool - so
he uses them to do thing that will hurt player B not being aware of
plyaaer A's surprise Life Boon - sort of the same thing. Player A
may not have five plus life boon to give player C, he was only going
to help player C survive for one more turn.

One thing player A could do is call a judge over and have him make
player C cease what he's doing without explaining why. That, at
least, may give him a chance of not getting a visit from Mr. Tho.

Was there time set aside for constructing your deck? There should have
been a specific time limiit. If you used _that_ time for sleeving
your deck, there should be no problem. Otherwise, you may have to
wait until another game. (There should certainly be enough time
between games to sleeve a deck.) As for time spent reading the cards,
if it's a problem, there should be a time limit. If there's no
specific time limit, it seems like it's neither here nor there
regardless of who did or didn't complain.

Fred

> if they had a problem, in such an open forum, would make them feel

You always have an opprtunity to lodge a complaint in private--it seems
highly likely that if anyone had lodged a complaint either publicly or
privately, it would have been rectified. As it was.

For my money, I understand why even reprinted new release cards are not
allowed for 30 days, as they might have different text that would cause some
confusion. This makes sense to me. This being said, I am completely
unconcerned with whether or not my opponents have, like, extra hard to get
rares or more Blood Dolls as the result of them being in not yet allowed
starters, or whatever, and for my money, I'd be perfectly happy if you could
use new reprints immediately. But understanding the problem that could be
caused by new wording on cards, I accept the current plan (although, it
isn't any more confusing to use non re-worded old cards, like Jyhad Wakes,
or whatever). In the situation as it occured, I was perfectly happy to see
people play with the cards they were using, even if they were from the new
set, as it made everyone's life easier. I would have expected someone who
had a problem with it, however, to make their concerns known. And someone
did, and it was fixed.

> argument with 30 other players. The tournament organizer did state that the
> cards were "common" or "nothing special" or something like that, which I
> guess was code for "It's not a Call the Great Beast deck," but it really
> wasn't fair to the players who paid attention to the rules and made certain
> to bring only legal decks. I'm glad this decision was reversed, thanks to
> you & Scott for taking the initiative.

Yeah, see, I certainly wouldn't have argued with you in a public forum--if
anyone had stood up and said "Hey. I don't like this." in regards to the
suggestion, I would have been completely ok with that, and likely would have
defended them saying that if anyone took issue with it, as it is the actual
rules, as that is why the actual rules are there.

This being said, in this forum, where it isn't actually an issue, why would
you have a problem with letting it slide, given that it simply made the
tournament work better? Heck, even if it *was* a deck using 6 KMW Call the
Great Beasts?

I suspect that most of the illegal cards were things like Blood Doll and
whatever (my pal Steve needed some cards for his deck right before the
tournament, picked up a KMW starter to get some, like, Swallowed by the
Nights or whatever, realized right before the gig that they were illegal and
swapped for non illegal copies, but I suspect that a bunch of people did the
same thing except without the realization and trading), but even if they
weren't, really, how is that a problem?



It's as simple as this: There are published rules. Regardless of the logic
of the rules on this issue, the rules are clear. Ten minutes prior to the
start of a tournament is not the time to debate or change these rules. A
sanctioned tournament, particularly a continental qualifier, should follow
the rules.

As to why I didn't complain on the scene before Eric & Scott took action,
think of the number of "name" players who were in attendance... I've been
playing for roughly 5 years but am a relative noob on the tournament scene.
I'm not going to stand up and make myself look like a jerk in front of that
many people who are so much more experienced than I. Nor am I going to
bother to protest in private to the organizer, who has better things to do
than listen to me when he's trying to get the first round started.

Messages.Author: Jozxyqk
Messages.Body:
echia...@yahoo.com wrote:

> #2. At the 2005 Northeast Qualifier in Mansfield, Massachusetts, there
> was initially a problem because a handful of players had included
> reprinted cards from the Kindred Most Wanted expansion in their decks
> (the cards were reprints from the starters but the problem is that none
> of the Kindred Most Wanted cards, even reprinted ones, were legal yet).

I waffled on this issue because I really felt bad having to tell players,
"You have a Kindred Most Wanted version of Blur in your deck, therefore
you are disqualified and can not play."
Especially since one player stated to me that he specifically went out of
his way to replace all of his older versions with the KMW versions where
he could that morning, just so that his deck would "look more up to date".

I understand the reasons for KMW-printing cards not being legal; but when
I saw which cards they were in each of the "offending" decks, I chose to
"let it slide but let everyone know" for time-saving reasons.
However, when people *did* voice their concern and came to me, the situation
was taken care of, and no KMW-printing cards were in players' decks when
play began.

Yes, people should absolutely know the vekn deck construction rules before
arriving at a tournament, and yes I will be more strict about it the next
time I'm running a Continental Qualifier the week after the release of a
new set that includes reprints.

> #3 [The Life Boon Situation]

There was really nothing that could have been done differently, after
the player began scooping up his belongings. He shouldn't have done so, but
if table-talk reveals that there's a Life Boon in someone's hand, there's
nothing illegal about other players taking advantage of that knowledge...

And just because "Anson Anarch Revolt" screams out "There is probably a Life
Boon in his hand" to many players, doesn't mean you can fault the scooping
player for not drawing that conclusion; different players have different
levels of experience and expertise with the game.

> #4 [Issues with the Sunday Draft]

As this was billed as a Prerelease, it wasn't under the governance of any
V:EKN rules. I ran it extremely informally, as it was entirely for fun
and the acquisition of "free stuff".
I made sure that everyone was finished constructing their decks before
beginning, except for the one issue of a player sleeving his draft deck.
The other players were itching to begin, so I gave that player's table
a few extra minutes to their 2 hour round, which they ended up not needing
anyway.

This was a learning experience for me, as my first large-scale event as
Prince. I'm glad that things went as smoothly as they did but I know
I can do certain things better next time.

Josh "Jozxyqk" Feuerstein
Prince of Boston

Bad thing. Should not happen. I strongly suggest you file a complaint

Well, the 5th player in New Jersey got lucky, and the 9th in Boston got
unlucky. All because of you... Shame.

> #2. At the 2005 Northeast Qualifier in Mansfield, Massachusetts, there
> was initially a problem because a handful of players had included
> reprinted cards from the Kindred Most Wanted expansion in their decks
> (the cards were reprints from the starters but the problem is that none
> of the Kindred Most Wanted cards, even reprinted ones, were legal yet).

I cannot disagree with this enough. Why would anyone in their right mind
complain about reprints? They are the same cards, only with different
layouts and expansion symbols. Seems pretty childish to me. (Not you in
general, just the behaviour).

> Now I understand that this is a difficult situation. If it were to
> happen again, this is what I would suggest: Player A does not say
> anything about having a way to save Player C, and simply allows Player
> C to pack up. When Player B ends his turn, and the Anarch Revolts would
> oust Player C, Player A plays the Life Boon. Reconstruct the game state
> as best as possible but if the previous game state could not be fully
> established then just let Player C sit there as a pool buffer. Since
> Player C had already given up, treat him as if he were not going to
> bother taking any actions or blocking.

Fair enough. Though the player controlling Le Din could've foreseen it,
and preemptively check to see the master deck's hand, just as the ousted
player could've anticipated it.

> The lesson from this experience is please please please don't
> completely pack up unless you are actually ousted. Or if you really do
> want to give up and pack up, be okay with "doing nothing" during
> your turn if you miraculously do survive.

Or just transfer out. Don't pack unless you are ousted; if you see no
chance, wait for your turn, and then transfer out. Or offer to concede
the game. There are options.

> #4. During the Starter/Draft event following the Northeast Qualifier, I
> am not sure if sufficient time was given for deck construction. Now
> please note that I *was* on time for the event (surprise, surprise). I
> was playing the Alastors deck and I didn't make many changes (took
> out 3 library cards and 1 crypt card, added a dozen library cards and 3
> or 4 crypt cards) so I *know* I did not spend a lot of time actually
> constructing my deck. Instead, I knew that I would have to spend most
> of the deck construction time sleeving my deck instead. Now some of my
> fellow players *strongly* expressed their dissatisfaction regarding the
> time I was taking to sleeve my deck. I feel that I was unfairly singled
> out.

Well, it is hard to judge this without knowing how much time was
*objectively* spent on this. Did you somehow offend the players who
"singled you out"? It is possible that they were just frustrated by
you somehow, and found an excuse. I'm not sure, I don't like draft,
and I don't really like being mean to others before the games. (During
the game, I sometimes do those things, but not before - I like fellow
VTES players, even if I can sometimes be a bit tenser at a game table.)

> Yes, I did need some time to fully prepare my deck. On the other
> hand however, I am an extremely fast and efficient drafter. Having
> previously played in two KMW pre-releases, I was already fairly
> familiar with most of the cards we were drafting.

I think though that you had an unfair advantage here. Nobody should
be allowed to participate in more than a single prerelease event for
any given set. Your example is good to show that being acquainted
with the set gives you an unfair advantage over the other players.

--
Bye,

Daneel

> The time limits must be set in advance of the tournament, and the

Cutting out the part about limited play, 3.1.1 reads:

"Each round in the tournament has a time limit. The minimum time limit
used in V:TES rounds is two hours. The time limit must be announced before
play begins. The final round may last longer than the preliminary rounds,
at the judge's option.

<limited stuff>

"The judge must announce when only 5 minutes remain in the current round.
When the round is over the judge will direct all players to put their
cards down. All play must immediately cease."

It's certainly logical that all preliminary rounds would be of the same
length, but I don't get that out of "each round in the tournament has a
time limit." That doesn't say "each round has the same time limit" to me
so much as says "each round will end at some point." "The time limit must
be announced" part could be interpreted as meaning "the time limit for
each round must be announced before play of those rounds begin."

In fact, that's what the judge for that event thought it did mean. When a
player objected to the shortened round, the judge stated that he'd
announced the time limit prior to the round beginning (true - I'd heard
him even if everyone else hadn't) and quoted 3.1.1 to support his
decision.

Regardless of whether a mistake was made, 3.1.1 could probably be more
clear.

Additionally, if we're going to be sticklers, I only rarely hear the five
minute warning at tournaments and that's usually only when someone asks.

Matt Morgan

Yes, I definitely agree with you (and the current rules) regarding not
allowing new cards (including reprinted ones) to be legal for 30 days.

#1. As you noted, the most important is regarding any text changes. New
copies with new text might be very confusing.

#2. Allowing *some* of the new set cards to be used but not others (say
allowing reprinted cards to be used but not "new" ones) can be
problematic. Especially if there's confusion, "I *thought* this card
was a reprint..." It's easier to just have a blanket "don't use cards
with this expansion symbol" rule (with an exception to some promos that
might have been released earlier).

#3. 30 days is a reasonable amount of time to ensure everyone has
sufficient time to access the new cards. It might have seemed odd if
right after Heidelberg, someone showed up with an Army of Nephandi deck
using the new not-yet-legal version. Or if someone attends a Saturday
Pre-Release and then plays in a Saturday night tournament using all of
the new reprints. (Not only is he using cards that aren't legal yet,
but they aren't even officially released yet!). Etc.

In short, the 30-day rule is there for a good reason and I definitely
think it should stay in place.

- Eric Chiang

>

> be allowed to participate in more than a single prerelease event
for
> any given set. Your example is good to show that being acquainted
> with the set gives you an unfair advantage over the other players.

I disagree that this constitutes an "unfair advantage." I knew several
of the other players at the event who had also attended two KMW
pre-releases.

Restricting players to a single pre-release is a bad idea for several
reasons.

- Since pre-releases are non-sanctioned (and there may be a variation
of rules/procedures/format), not a lot of detailed record-keeping is
done. Requiring detailed reports to make sure players don't attend
multiple events just adds to the work overhead that White Wolf and VEKN
already have to deal with.

- Such a restriction would decrease participation and weaken the
relationships between different playgroups. At least in my area, there
was quite a lot of proliferation among different playgroups for the
different pre-releases. It really helps in building bridges and
reaching out to other groups.

In addition, being "acquainted with the set" as a result of playing in
a pair of pre-releases isn't necessarily a significant advantage. A
different player could easily gather as much info by reading the
spoilers on the newsgroup. Should players also be banned from accessing
the newsgroup prior to such an event? Hmmm...maybe the best solution is
to require players to remain in a sensory deprivation chamber for 30
days prior to the event. That way they won't be able to gain an unfair
advantage...

To further elaborate, why is it an "unfair advantage" to have attended
previous events? On that basis, maybe Josh Duffin and Ben Peal should
be banned from all limited draft events. Since they have played so many
limited games, surely they have an "unfair advantage", especially if
they play in a limited event with a newbie. ::sighs::

- Eric Chiang

Yep. Sometimes when I'm bored I play Yahoo Chess. In Yahoo Chess, if
you make a mistake, you can request a takeback. In that case, a box
appears on your opponent's screen telling him that you're requesting a
takeback and he has the option to allow it or not.

Whenever someone requests a takeback, it's a red flag for something out
of the ordinary. There have been plenty of times when I did not
initially realize that my opponent had made a critical mistake. But
then when he asks for a takeback, I think "hey, something is up" which
makes me scrutinize the situation more carefully.

As a result, whenever I make a mistake of my own, I find it's better to
just hope that my opponent misses it, as opposed to alerting him that
something is out of the ordinary and putting me at the mercy of whether
he'll let me take back the move. (Since this is Chess, note that these
are PLAY mistakes, not RULE mistakes).

- Eric Chiang

It seems to me that the reason for the "no cards, even reprints, within 30
days of set release" rule is mainly that in any given set, WW *could* change
the cardtext of *all* the reprints. Sure, it's not terribly hard to
remember that Anarch Revolt and Heart of Darkness were changed in KMW, and
so those copies of new cards wouldn't be legal until 30 days out while the
rest would - but it does have the potential to be a problem, if more cards
are changed.

that don't do what they say is almost as bad as newer printings that don't
(yet) do what they say, it seems to me that this problem (cards not doing
what they say) is one that it's better not to exacerbate any more than
necessary. (I probably wouldn't have changed Heart of Darkness's text, if
it were up to me, for example. ;-)

> is tournaments starting late and ending late. I realize this is usually
> considered a courtesy to the folks running a little behind, but it's
> also a big "fuck you" to people who have to leave the event promptly.

"Leave the event promptly"? What IS "(leaving) the event promptly"?
You sound as if you think there's some gurantee of how long an event
should take. If you attend an event that's billed as 2R + F with all
two-hour time limits and begins at noon, you shouldn't be planning on
leaving by 6:30 or 7 PM. There could be any number of delays,
particularly including rules debates that take time to resolve and
thus extend a round's timing considerably.

Where your pet peeve is valid, IME, has to do with tournaments bending
over backwards to accommadate the late people so far that it's sort
of abusive to the prompt people - those who showed up on time and are
now sitting around, bored, because they thought a tournament was
supposed to start at noon (or whatever time it was scheduled). Worse,
this sends the message that lateness is tolerated and expected, so
people stop bothering to show up on time at all - after all, why show
up spot on noon if it's just more time you're going to spend sitting
around waiting for others to show up?

I'm a habitually late person myself, though I make an effort to defeat
that inclination whenever possible. Thus, I really like it when a
tournament organizer is understanding about lateness and doesn't just
drop you like a hot potatoe if you walk in 30 seconds late. Or even
holds things up if someone calls his cell and tells him he'll show up
in another 5 or 10 minutes. But if it starts getting to be the better
part of an hour or so waiting for someone who promised to show up and
isn't here and no one's heard from him, that's abusive of the people
who bothered to be on time.

Fred

I don't like the plutocentrism here. All of the not-quite-legal cards were
proxies. A player who shows up with 20 brand new War Ghoul reprints isn't
breaking the rules any more than someone who shows up with one Blood Doll
reprint and there's no good reason to draw a line between them.

The difference here is intent. A player who puts the not-quite-legal cards
in his deck puts them in there because he mistakenly believes they are
legal (or because he is cheating). A player who puts in cards that are
blatantly not what they say they are is cheating.

In the case of the NEQ, it was determined that the players who put KMW
cards in were not cheating and that is the only reason why they were
allowed to use the cards.

Sorry, Ankur. My newsreading service is usually pretty good but I just
can't find any previous post you'd made in this thread. I'll address the
things I've seen people (possibly you) say about this.

I agree that unequal access to new cards is probably a good reason for the
30 day rule in general. Where reprints are concerned, however, the rule is
just more problem than it's worth. This is a judgement thing and I'll
freely admit this is just my opinion. But:

1) I don't see the point of worrying about someone's access to a KMW Dreams of
the Sphinx when there are already legal copies of Dreams of the Sphinx in
circulation. If you want to point to one person's superior ability to get
a new KMW Dreams of the Sphinx over someone else, I will point backwards at
some players who have been playing longer having likewise a superior ability
to get old Dreams of the Sphinx in comparison to newer players. I just don't
care about this.

It's a good rule for new cards. Plus, there's several other good reasons to
apply it to new cards such as giving players and judges the chance to learn
about new cards and giving LSJ the chance to rule on and make known his
rulings on new cards that have new abilities and affect the game in hitherto
unknown ways. But it's not worth bothering with for reprints.

2) It causes confusion. People see that a card's a reprint, they expect it
to be legal to play because it already _is_ legal to play in other forms.
What happened at the NE Regional Qualifier is a classic example. Of course,
people should know the deck construction rules and I'm not making excuses.
But every nuance you throw into the deck construction rules is one more
detail people will tend to forget occasionally and when they do, it causes
problems. So if it's not a necessary nuance - get rid of it for the common
good. I don't feel this is a necessary nuance.

Probably not the most important issue in the world, I'll grant. But there
you are.

Fred

Messages.Author: Xian
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
> I agree that unequal access to new cards is probably a
> good reason for the 30 day rule in general. Where
> reprints are concerned, however, the rule is just more
> problem than it's worth. This is a judgement thing and
> I'll freely admit this is just my opinion. But:

Surely it's easier to draw a line in the sand, and simply rule out any
cards from the newest set. Adherence to it can be easily verified by
checking for the symbol from the new set.

That way, assuming you are holding a constructed tournament within the
first 30 days after a set is released, you don't have to carefully dig
through each deck to verify that card X isn't in there, but if you find
card Y, it's okay. (Assuming you were going to do that in the first
place.)

I agree that it's a little nitpicky, but the current setup probably
avoids more problems than it creates.

As far as causing confusion re: reprints, surely the possibility exists
that allowing "reprints" to be playable, but not "new" cards, you would
either have to define what is a reprint in the new set or rely on
players to make that distinction. Assuming the latter, I can imagine a
case where a new player finds a neat "new" card (that is in fact, a
reprint of a card that newbie hasn't seen before) and wants to build a
deck around it but doesn't. Then in the tournament sees someone else
playing with it, and rails against the old boys network/knowledge that
clued other people into the fact that card X was a reprint, but he
didn't know of.

I guess I just think that if a clear distinction can be drawn, it's
easier to take that route (no cards from the new set) than to divide it
up into (reprints are okay, unless they're functionally changed). I'm
not sure you were arguing that latter point, but that's presumably the
way it would have to go.

Xian

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
echia...@yahoo.com wrote:

>A.) Should reprinted cards obtained through a pre-release be legal
>immediately?

Yes.

>B.) In the past there have been occasions when a set was made available
>even before the pre-release. For example, for the Black Hand expansion,
>cards were first available at some White Wolf sponsored LARP Con. Now
>this was over a week before even the pre-releases (which were in turn a
>few days before the set was officially released). In such an occasion,
>should the reprinted cards be legal immediately?

Yes.

>C.) If cards were obtained illegally before the official release date
>(say someone broke into the White Wolf warehouse and stole the new
>cards), should they be tournament legal immediately?

I don't see any reason why not. Other than, like, for legal reasons
involving posession of stolen goods. But that has nothing to do with game
play.

> So...where do you want to draw the line in the sand? And why do you
> think this line is better than the one already drawn?

I think the proposed line is fairly clear--functionally identical reprints
are legal as soon as you have them in your posession, be it from a
pre-release, a pre-pre-release, or a knocked over delivery truck. *When* the
cards get to you is irrelevant--a Blood Doll is a Blood Doll is a Blood
Doll, regardless of the date of release.

New cards or changed cards should not be legal for 30 days, but as proposed
by various folks, functionally identical reprints should be legal at all
times.

For my money, that reprinted cards are extra available from a new set in
starters, or whatever, is irrelevant. That someone has theoretically
"easier" access to Call the Great Beast or Dreams of the Sphinx in starters
from the new set has no impact, in my mind, on competetive play. If someone
can, the day a new set comes out, go out and buy enough starters to build a
Call the Great Beast deck and use it in a tournament the next day? More
power to them--there were already Call the Great Beasts available to him, so
I see no functional difference between buying ten CtGB for $20.00 each off
of E-bay or buying ten CtGB in starters.

There is an argumant to be made, certainly, that the current system is
easier--just *all* cards from a given set are illegal for 30 days, which
prevents confusion from new and re-written cards before everyone has seen
them, and this easy system leaves us with functionally identical reprints
getting swept up in the easy fix. But personally, I don't think there really
is any reasonable justification, other than "it's just easier that way", to
keep people from using functionally identical reprints from a new set
immediately. Granted, "it's just easier that way" is a not insignificant
argument, but I'd much rather see a system of "new cards and newly worded
cards are illegal for 30 days, functionally identical reprints are legal
immediately", 'cause I see no significant reason other than "it's just
easier that way" to keep them out of play for those 30 days.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:

> I'm confused why you think any line needs to be drawn. Er, except the
> illegal thing.

Illegalities aside, I find it refreshing that Fred and I are on the apparent
exact same page here :-)

Eric is looking for a line, and as I mentioned earlier, I think the line is
an easy one to draw--functionally identical reprints (cards with the same
name and functionally the same text) should be legal for play as soon as you
get them in your grubby little hands. New cards and cards with new wording
should be illegal for 30 days.

See, there are two, essentntially exclusive, issues at hand here:

A) New cards and newly worded cards are confusing and potentially unfair to
people who haven't seen them yet in competetive play. This strikes me as a
perfectly reasonable issue, that is addressed by having new and reworded
cards illegal for 30 days. Makes perfect sense to me.

B) Access to old cards in new sets is somehow unfair to people who don't
have access to the new cards yet. This strikes me as a preposterous issue.
The above issue (i.e. issue "A") is perfectly logical and has a direct
impact on competetive play--if I haven't managed, for whatever reason, to be
able to get ahold of the new set, it makes sense that I'd be concerned about
being surprised by totally new cards and new wording, and 30 days seems like
a reasonable amount of time to gain access to new cards, or at least see the
spoilers. On the other hand, that someone has cheap and easy access to
Dreams of the Sphinx or Call the Great Beast in a new starter deck strikes
me as totally irrelevant to game play--one could argue, sure, that it is
somehow unfair to be able to buy Dreams or Call in a starter that someone
else might not have access to for whatever reason, but this line of argument
falls very short for me, as *everyone already has access to Dreams and
Call*, and the difference between "I can buy a starter and get a Dreams or a
Call for $10.00 easy!" and "I can get a Dreams or Call on e-bay for $20.00,
easy!" is not one that is worth quibbling over.

Again, there is also the argument of "it is just easier this way" (i.e. ban
the whole set for 30 days), which isn't an insignificant argument. But
really, the confusion of "Anarch Revolt doesn't use the new wording for a
few more weeks..." is no greater than "Anarch Revolt doesn't use the old
wording anymore...", for my money, and doesn't really justify totally
preventing the use of functionally identical reprints as soon as you get
them.

Just as a very concrete but minor example, at the NEQ, my pal Steve (that
would be Steve "I Bled Someone for 14 in One Turn 'Cause of Stupid
Misdirection" Wampler) came to play, but doesn't have a lot of cards, as
most of his VTES stuff was stolen out of his car a few years back. He just
recently got into the game again, and went to go play at the NEQ with the
cards he had. He realized right before the event that he needed various
common cards for the deck he wanted to play, went to the dealers room, and
picked up a couple KMW starters (the only cards available to buy) so he
could get some Swallowed by the Nights or something. He put them in his
deck, got to the event, realized that the KMW cards were illegal, and spent
a frantic 15 minutes trading around with various people for legal copies of
the cards. He lucked out and found folks to swap with, but the whole venture
was absurd--it made no sense at all, at least in my mind, that he should
have to swap for legal Swalloweds and Behind You's when he had cards to use
in his hands already, but they were arbitrarily illegal.

Messages.Author: lehrbuch
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
> There is an argumant to be made, certainly, that the current system
> is easier--just *all* cards from a given set are illegal for 30 days,
> which prevents confusion from new and re-written cards before
> everyone has seen them, and this easy system leaves us with
> functionally identical reprints getting swept up in the easy fix.

I think that "it's easier" is a pretty convincing argument for keeping
the current system. It resolves any issue about what "functionally
identical" means. This is more complicated than it first appears.

Obviously, an identical card is "functionally identical".

Is a card that has identical text, but different art work "functionally
identical"?

Is a card that has different text, but text which follows previous
errata "functionally identical"?

Is a reprint that contains different punctuation "functionally identical"?

Is a reprint that includes redundant clarification text "functionally
identical"?

Is "Reverend Djoser Jones" "functionally identical" to "Khalil Anvari"?

Were the various Investment cards "functionally identical" when they
were reprinted with the key word "Investment"? The key word had no
effect until other cards (Alan Sovereign) become legal.

There is much more scope for argument and confusion if "functionally
identical" cards become immediately legal. Judges will need to make
more decisions, or WW/LSJ will need to list those cards which are
"functionally identical" - either will lead to arguments over the
cornercase decisions.

I'd rather that the appropriate forums were filled after a new release
with comments/arguments/clarifications about the *new* cards in the set
- rather than long-term irrelevant arguments over whether reprints are
functionally identical or not.

If you're worried about reprint legality: don't hold, or compete in, a
pre-constructed event 30 days after a release date. Issue solved.

--
* lehrbuch (lehr...@gmail.com)

> Eric is looking for a line, and as I mentioned earlier, I think the
line is

unfair to

as a
> perfectly reasonable issue, that is addressed by having new and
reworded
> cards illegal for 30 days. Makes perfect sense to me.

Yes, but then there's the issue of what a "functionally identical
reprint" vs. "cards with new wording" is. Of course it's obvious that
in KMW, Anarch Revolt and Heart of Darkness have new wording (they got
a special little mention). But in the past, there have been several
cases when stealth errata occurs or a slight change of wording means
that the card works differently now.

For example, take a look at the "Updated Reprints" list in the
Camarilla Expansion section. Notice that it does not list any of the
functional changes to Burst of Sunlight, Cryptic Rider, Eagle's Sight,
Charnas the Imp, and Kiss of Ra that occurred in that set and were only
discovered later. What would have happened if someone tried playing a
reprinted version of one of these cards at a tournament, not knowing
that the text was subtly changed? (And unfortunately, not every
tournament and player will have access to the Internet and older
editions of every card during the tournament).

I haven't had a chance to thoroughly examine the KMW set yet to see if
there are additional wording changes but someone already posted a
question about the new Psychomachia (see a previous thread about
Bloodstorm and Psychomachia). See how much confusion that caused? LSJ's
gut reaction was to reverse the previous ruling on Psychomachia due to
the new text (though he later reinstated it). Think of the chaos this
could cause at a standard tournament with a normal judge!

Now of course, in an ideal world, White Wolf would be able to inform us
of all these nitty-gritty changes. But sometimes slipups aren't caught.
Sometimes some other guy in charge of wording or layout drops the ball
at the last minute. Sometimes one can't determine all of the
corner-case ramifications that might result from clarifying and
rewording some card text. Overall LSJ and White Wolf do a great job and
to expect such perfection is unrealistic.

I don't suppose you recall all of the rampant card text migrations from
the SW and FN era? Although most of those changes were good, it does
take time to find and digest these modifications. In the 10th
Anniversary Edition, there were mistakes to the printing of Hell Hound
and Business Pressure which were clarified only later. There were also
several card text migrations which weren't announced by LSJ on the
newsgroup until December 2nd, 2004. Since the cards were available in
Heidelberg before that, it's still a 4-5 day window when people could
have been playing with reprinted cards with functionally new text,
without knowing that there was a change.

So back to the original issue, I wanted to point out that the concern
about "reprints with new text" isn't just a small microcosm of all the
cards. Just because we are aware that AR and Heart of Darkness were
changed doesn't mean that there aren't other changes lurking around the
corner. Allowing these cards to be instantly legal is bound to cause a
great deal of confusion as a result. Previous sets reveal how many
reprinted cards can have subtle new changes. And that is why a 30-day
waiting period for both completely new and also reprinted cards
(whether we think there is old text or not) is entirely appropriate.

- Eric Chiang

Messages.Author: Jozxyqk
Messages.Body:
[People wrote stuff about which cards should be legal in less than 30 days,
and I chose an arbitrary place to jump back into the thread]

If it *is* a question of rarity, then what is the difference between the
legality of Kindred Most Wanted cards, and the legality of a new print
run of Sabbat War after a year of being out of print, for example?
Surely this makes the "availability" argument fall flat on its face, since
this hypothetical reprint of Sabbat War has suddenly made Direct Intervention
or War Ghouls or whatever "more common" than they'd been for the time SW was
not being printed. That reprint is no different than a "brand new expansion"
with no functional changes to the cards it did reprint; it's irrelevant that
it happens to have no brand new cards. And the familiar expansion symbol
only makes it impossible to judge whether the card is "30 days old" or not.

However, my main point is parallel to the rules per se:
Much like I have never seen a judge call someone out for having
an "improper mix" of Jyhad vs VTES-backed cards, I would like to remind
everyone that this is a game. And the attendees to tournaments, in general,
are primarily there to play the game they love and to have fun.

So if situations like these arise, regardless of what the letter of the law
says, just LET IT GO!
Cheating is one thing. But accidentally putting a reprint in your deck, or
putting 2 Jyhad-backed cards in your library, or bringing a vampire out
in the middle of your influence phase before you're done transferring.. come
on, people, these are not worth punishing for. There is no need for
nitpicky anal-retentive judges who are going to disqualify someone who made
an innocent mistake.

I hadn't made any previous posts. I was referring to others' arguments.

> I agree that unequal access to new cards is probably a good reason for
> the 30 day rule in general. Where reprints are concerned, however, the
> rule is just more problem than it's worth. This is a judgement thing
> and I'll freely admit this is just my opinion. But:

I think it's possible for a player not to realize that a card is a
reprint. Or that the text of a reprinted card is notably different from
the old text that it is in effect a new card. What's the simplest and most
universal way then to incorporate the "generally good reason" for the 30
day rule for new cards? That's right -- all cards are restricted for 30
days.

> 1) I don't see the point of worrying about someone's access to a KMW
> Dreams of the Sphinx when there are already legal copies of Dreams of
> the Sphinx in circulation. If you want to point to one person's
> superior ability to get a new KMW Dreams of the Sphinx over someone
> else, I will point backwards at some players who have been playing
> longer having likewise a superior ability to get old Dreams of the
> Sphinx in comparison to newer players. I just don't care about this.

My point isn't about accessibility, though since I sent you gallavanting
off onto other people's posts, I can't really blame you for that. :)

> It's a good rule for new cards. Plus, there's several other good
> reasons to apply it to new cards such as giving players and judges the
> chance to learn about new cards and giving LSJ the chance to rule on and
> make known his rulings on new cards that have new abilities and affect
> the game in hitherto unknown ways. But it's not worth bothering with
> for reprints.

I'm not sure that the judging concerns are that meaningful. Theoretically
speaking, you'll still have a number of rules clarifications for the first
few tournaments after a set has been released.

> 2) It causes confusion. People see that a card's a reprint, they expect
> it to be legal to play because it already _is_ legal to play in other
> forms. What happened at the NE Regional Qualifier is a classic example.

What may also cause confusion is the converse -- players not knowing what
is and isn't a reprint. I've got a group with lots of new players, and it
would be a *nightmare* to tell them which cards were and weren't legal
from the set. And even if you did, you might have other problems based on
how similar the cards sound. Suppose for instance that there was a new
card called "Spectral Intervention". That's really close to "Spectral
Divination" and "Spiritual Intervention" (two names that many players mix
up). Now you'd have the issue of "but I thought it was legal and I put in
437 copies into my deck and now what do I do cause I can't play anymore".
Gosh, I'd hate to be the guy to have to remind/clarify to a (relatively)
newer player which cards to include.

Ultimately, allowing reprints favors those who have been playing long
enough to know what the reprints are. Not allowing them favors the other
group. My two points are this: 1) the simple universal approach for the
"generally good reason" is consistent and does the job, and 2) players who
know what are/aren't reprints can be expected to care more about such
things as deck construction in general.

> Of course, people should know the deck construction rules and I'm not
> making excuses. But every nuance you throw into the deck construction
> rules is one more detail people will tend to forget occasionally and
> when they do, it causes problems. So if it's not a necessary nuance -
> get rid of it for the common good. I don't feel this is a necessary
> nuance.

Apply this very same logic to a different demographic of people, and
you'll see a whole host of considerations which support the
counter-argument. Except that *that* demographic has more of an excuse to
not know deck construction rules than others.

Ankur

"Ankur Gupta" <agu...@cs.duke.edu> wrote in message

>> I agree that unequal access to new cards is probably a good reason for

>> rule is just more problem than it's worth. This is a judgement thing
>> and I'll freely admit this is just my opinion. But:
>
> I think it's possible for a player not to realize that a card is a
> reprint.

On some level, players have to understand there's a 30 day limitation for
new cards. If a player doesn't understand THAT, he'll only create a
legal deck by chance.

If a player does know about the rule, this isn't a problem. It's a very
simple rule to follow: if you know that a card of the same name already
exists, you can use it. If not, you'd better not - or go check with
someone else who knows about past printings.

It doesn't matter. It's not a very hard rule to follow either way.

> Or that the text of a reprinted card is notably different from
> the old text that it is in effect a new card.

They may not know that the text of an old card has been errated, either.
Or that it's been changed by a more recent printing. The problem of
ignorance about what the functional text of a given card is already
exists. And this situation really isn't the worst one by far: to
play the card, a player has to at least know that former version of
it existed. He should go a little further and make sure that he knows
what those versions did - which is what he should do for all the cards
he uses anyway.

>> 2) It causes confusion. People see that a card's a reprint, they expect
>> it to be legal to play because it already _is_ legal to play in other
>> forms. What happened at the NE Regional Qualifier is a classic example.
>
> What may also cause confusion is the converse -- players not knowing what
> is and isn't a reprint. I've got a group with lots of new players, and it
> would be a *nightmare* to tell them which cards were and weren't legal
> from the set.

See above. I have no idea what's nightmarish about it. It's pretty simple.

> And even if you did, you might have other problems based on
> how similar the cards sound. Suppose for instance that there was a new
> card called "Spectral Intervention". That's really close to "Spectral
> Divination" and "Spiritual Intervention" (two names that many players mix
> up).

This seems overstated to me. If you stop and think about new players
considering using a reprint card, it shouldn't be hard to figure out if
it's legal or not and get it right. In most expansions (things like
Camarilla Edition aside), they should know they can't use anything from
the booster packs. The only things they can use are from precons and
then only after checking to see if a card is a reprint. Probably they'd
want to know from what previous edition and if the card text was the same.
If they're considering using a new card they have no knowledge because they
suspect it might be a reprint, they know they have to investiage its
legality anyway so they should be alert enough to do it right. If they
HAVE knowledge of the existing card in previous editions, then they know
they have the right one and they know what it does - including if the new
wording has changes.

I just can't imagine how this could cause problems. It never seemed to in
Magic.

> Ultimately, allowing reprints favors those who have been playing long
> enough to know what the reprints are.

If you don't know what the reprints are, you don't know about the card
anyway, so I fail to see the issue. I think the knowledge issue tends
to favor older players anyway - for much better reasons than that they're
aware they can use a new expansion reprint card right away. So I'm going
to wave my hand over this issue. ("Go away,...go away!" :-) ) I don't
think it's much.

> My two points are this: 1) the simple universal approach for the
> "generally good reason" is consistent and does the job, and 2) players who
> know what are/aren't reprints can be expected to care more about such
> things as deck construction in general.

OK, I don't understand this. So I can't respond.

Fred

Fair enough.

I would have said: all unique cards contest with identically named
cards, they function identically in this regard. Therefore "Khalil"
contests with "Khalil" and "The Reverend" contests with "The Reverend".

Phrasing the contestion functionality carefully makes them appear to be
functionally identical. Hence, why a single description of contestion
in the rulebook (4.1) suffices, rather than hundreds of "X contests
copies of X", "Y contests copies of Y", "Z contests copies of Z" statements.

functionally identical or not can be contentious. Hence, why it's a
good idea to have the current not-legal-for-30-days clause - to prevent
needing to make this decision.

Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:
Hey Daneel, if you're looking for a less-abrasive look at similar points
of the opposition, see my exchange with Fred on this same thread. Replace
Fred with you, Derek with me, and now you've got a conversation that ain't
fraught with anger and viciousness.

And here's someone who's piping in definitively -- I've taught lots of
newbies. And I can assure you from repeated efforts that it's just
infinitely less complicated to follow a single one-stop rule that says,
"Hey, yeah! Look at that symbol up there! That's a not-so-good symbol for
the next 30 days!" <gets patted on the head by the local prince>

It's just that easy.

Ankur

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Ankur Gupta" <agu...@cs.duke.edu> wrote in messagenews:Pine.GSO.4.62.05...@peso.cs.duke.edu...

>>> So if they have to understand that, why not make it absolute rather
>>> than require yet another hoop to jump through?
>>

>> Please notice, there's two ways to look at an "inconsistency" here.
>> You can focus on the expansion symbol on the card or you can look at
>> whether the card's a reprint or a new card. You insist on suggesting
>> the focus is on the expansion symbol is the natural thing, you're going
>> to come to the conclusion that it's more complex to divide up whole sets
>> into the legal and the illegal.
>
> Well, I'm "insisting" upon that based upon a series of arguments around
> the fact that deciding whether something is a reprint or not is an
> additional step -- a step which is not necessarily trivial for certain
> (not-altogether-uncommon-or-pathological) cases.

Insist on it for any reason you want, just notice that it's not the only
way to view the situation, that other people "naturally" tend to view it
otherwise, and that an argument which asserts that ITS way of seeing
reality is the simplest one has a problem when real life evidence tends
to suggest otherwise.

> This basic point seems to
> be the point of our contention. Yes, experienced players (and thus, most
> of those who post here) will tend to think that it is far more natural and
> logical that reprints are legal. But I'm allowing for those who wouldn't
> necessarily have been posting here yet. . . you know, the new people.

Of course new people. That's who I'm talking about, too. Who else would
have shown up at the NE Qualifier with illegal decks?

> And besides that, how much more simple can it get than to look at card X.
> Without needing additional information, you *know* whether or not it's
> legal. Done. Finished. No more discussion. No exceptions. No conditions.

Sure. What makes you think it works any differently if you make the
determination from a card's *name* rather than it's expansion symbol.
Last I checked, the name was a visible attribute on a card, just like an
expansion symbol.

>>But many players seem to think otherwise, in my observation. The look
>
> Unless your observation includes a large demographic of players (read new)
> that are not currently represented in this argument, you're bound to come
> to a skewed conclusion.

Fine - then let's make no assumptions about it either way - in which case,
I don't want to here the argument that the existing system must be the
simplest one. I'm simply pointing out to you that some don't see that way
and here's evidence that maybe you're wrong - it's NOT the simplest way.

That and the fact that the DCI uses the system and doesn't seem to have
a problem with it.

> Hell, let me say this: I
> personally would be in favor of reprints being legal immediately.
> (Avoiding of course the sticky point of cards which have changed function
> in the newer printing.) But I recognize that it's better for the game, for
> the community, and for new players, not to add more complications. V:TES
> has a high learning curve. Takes weeks to learn the mechanics, and weeks
> more to follow the actions which are taken in a game. Some people after 10
> years of playing are still learning table dynamics. And yes, for new
> players, complications can include trying to find out if a card is a
> reprint.

Gee, I had no clue this reason was so 'important'. Truth is, I'm just
responding to your argument. Lest we lose perspective here, I don't think
it's that important a rule either way, as I said at the onset. But
obviously, I certainly don't think it's 'better' for the game for the
reason another poster brought up - people traveling to a tournament under
a misunderstanding that reprinted new copies shouldn't be a problem in their
decks and discovering at the last minute that it's not true. Clearly, that
happens, and I fail to see what is so 'important' about requiring them to
rework their decks at the last minute somehow (or worse, applying penalties
to them if discovered during play).

>>> No, that's not true. To play a card, one does not necessarily need to
>>> know that a former version existed.
>>
>> But to assume it's legal before the date, he does.
>
> There's that step we're talking about. The point where a player must know
> more to execute the more logical rule that you're talking about. . . . You
> know, I have players show up with invalid crypts for the first few
> weeks/months they play the game. And though I tell them, I also tell them
> that it's ok. It's because they simply *don't know*.

All right, I don't see the communication glitch here but we're clearly talking
past each other. If a player knows a previous version of the card is legal,
he CAN use it. If he's never seen it before but knows the reprint rule, he
won't TRY to use it - unless he takes the time to establish that it had been
previously printed. I fail to see any problems with any of this.

>>>> I have no idea what's nightmarish about it. It's pretty simple.
>>>
>>> Simple, sure. Time-consuming, though.
>>
>> Why the heck is it "time-consuming"?!? Look, it's REALLY simple: the
>> player has either seen the card before or he hasn't. If he hasn't seen
>> it, he should assume it's illegal. He only has to go further than that
>> if he's curious about it for some reason.
>
> What if he's seen it before, but it's a promo card, which is also not
> legal yet?

Huh?!? That's scratching. If a new player doesn't know a promo card is
not legal to play then he might play the promo card itself illegally - so
this is not a new problem. Answer to this by either system: player must know
the legal date to play all promo cards.

> What if he's seen it in someone else's box and isn't sure what
> set it was from? What if he's seen it in a dream with pink bunnies telling
> him that it's legal? Why not just have a one-stop check-it-here
> check-it-now solution? I mean, seriously? What's the rush?

Pretty much scratching on all of these. What if he sees a Return to
Innocence or Madness of the Bard in another player's box and has no idea
they're banned.

The rush is so not ban peoples' decks that don't need to be banned.

>> Unless you mean, players are going to look through all the precons and
>> start wondering if they can use any of these cards before March 23rd.
>> They can *ALREADY* do that! Only difference is that now, they'd have to
>> look through the precon, go find out if the card already exists in a
>> previous printing, AND have to go out and score an old version of a
>> card. It's actually MORE complicated NOW.
>
> No they don't. They look at the cards in the precon, and say, "Man, look
> at that conveniently-located set symbol here in the top right-hand corner
> of these cards. Gosh, can't play that for 30 days." DONE. You're the one
> making this complicated.

This is just ignoring a response and ducking back into the safety of your
original argument. And I will say, I've seen plenty of the reverse:
attempting to make the reprint-allowed proposal seem a zillion times more
complex than it is so I'm unrepentent about pointing out what's equally
"complex" under the existing system. The truth is, it's not all that
complicated either way - but coming to the grips with that point is causing
a lot more angst and frenetic hand-waving than it ought to.

>> Sorry. Don't mean to get impatient but this really isn't rocket
>> science.
>
> You're right. And I'm wondering how you're missing the point here.

Well, maybe it's because it's not as good of a point as you think?

>>> Assuming they're going to do some checking, yes. But remember who we're
>>> talking about: people who bring illegal decks to tournaments. Now, how
>>> do you get these people to bring valid decks? Make things simple.
>>
>> Let me ask you this: if this is all that complex, do you think the DCI

>

Well, gee then - if it's such complex rule as you claim, how does that
work with the 'simpler' game. That seems a bit of incongruous
explaination.

> Reprints are block-limited.

Oh for crying out loud - this has been true since the beginning. Since
Type 1 was THE tournament game. No one had trouble with it then and
"block limiting" has nothing to do with the issue.

> Most people who play Magic have played Magic before at some point.

Sorry, this is just a weird point. I'd say "Most people who play Jyhad
have play Jyhad before at some point." I don't know where you're going
with this.

> Magic doesn't have as complex card
> interactions as V:TES (or at least didn't when I was playing), which means
> that slightly different card texts have less of an impact than say, in
> V:TES.

I don't quibble over any of this. Sure, it's a different. But it works.
I think you're just scratching for points to evade just accepting that
the reprints-allowed rule works fine. It doesn't cause a ton of problems
like you're suggesting it might. I wish we could just agree on that
rather than quibbling about an issue that to me, seems in way in doubt.

>>> Too many assumptions Fred. No way new players will want to know if it's
>>> from a previous edition. At least, not necessarily.
>>
>> Then they won't suspect it's legal and won't use it, will they? How is
>> THIS a problem?!?
>
> So, wouldn't that newbie feel like it's a bit unfair that he could have
> used card X if he had just *known* it was legal?

No, not really. Sorry (...again), this seems a bit silly, conjecturing
'resentment'. Most normal people just slap their foreheads and say, "HEY!
I could have had a V8!" (Or a Dreams of the Sphinx...) If new-player-
seething-resentment over cards they could have played but didn't know
were legal, I'd advocate shooting them with tranquilizer guns. Aren't we
already using them when new players discover an OLD card they'd never seen
before and go berserk?

>>> I don't know how better to explain it. You snipped my point about the
>>> nuances argument you made applying to my case. . . . I don't know how
>>> else to demonstrate that according to our metric, simple is best
>>

>> Agreed. It's the definition of "simple" that I maintain needs work.
>> When real people tend to assume the opposite of the existing rule,
>> that's a good indication that it's not as "simple" as it could be.
>
> Again, you're not lookinng at the people who might be confused by this
> rule. You're only seeing experienced players.

Again, no, I'm talking about new players. I don't know why you think
I'm talking about experienced players. Experienced players know the rule
either way and don't bring illegal decks to tournaments.

> Right back at you Freddie boy. :)

Check. :-)

Fred

an
> expansion symbol.

It takes N card-checks to identify all not-yet-legal cards in your deck
if you merely have to check the expansion symbol (N being the number of
cards in your deck). It takes N card-checks and N database-lookups to
verify legality if you have to check card name. The database is also
not universally available (a checklist doesn't come in the starters).

have

Simplicity and intuition need not coincide. In fact, some people will
naturally assume that all Blood Dolls are legal, and assume that no KMW
cards (including reprints) are legal, and not realize that the
assumptions are contradictory until it's pointed out to them.



I agree that penalties should be minimal to nonexistant for such a
minor rules violation, yes. I'd also be fine with giving TDs the
authority to alter the rules (in advance) to allow reprints for the
sake of everyone's fun. That said, the default rule should be the
simpler case.




enough reason to put up with 30 days of irritation, IMO.

that

Not if you believe that the negative effects of complexity grow out of
proportion with complexity itself. A relatively simple game can survive
a few complex rules additions/changes. Once it acheives a certain
complexity, adding more rules of similar complexity adds a great deal
more frustration than the first few did.

Of course, you don't have to believe this. Even believing it, you don't
have to believe that VTES has reached such a point. That doesn't
invalidate the argument, though.

John

Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:

I understand your point regarding simplicity. I value simplicity. It is
important, but I think there may be more important things. What do you
think of the following:

In a perfect world the rule on unaltered reprints would be taken loosely.
The rule would exist, especially for the player's own good (not to
accidentally confuse reprints with new cards, for which the rule is
highly logical). Players who came to tournaments with unaltered
reprints from a set that is not tournament legal yet would be tolerated
without question, and noone would mind other players playing unaltered
reprints, as they are the same cards they already know, even if they
have a different expansion symbol.

We don't, however, live in a perfect world. So when people show up with
a KMW Blur or Blood Doll in their decks, some folks will actually
complain about that. They will see to the judge having to find proxies
for the reprinted cards. How does replacing a KMW Blur with a BH Blur
actually make ANY difference? This seems to be beyond pointlessness.

Of course, I see the general point of the rule, and I see the general
point of keeping rules if they exist, but this particular example is
just beyond me. Even if a rule is generally needed, and keeping rules
is generally good, doing something stupid is still doing something
stupid.

Aside, there's also the issue with new players needing the reprinted
copies. I'm not sure about this, but I would think that the new players
would especially value if they could use their freshly obtained cards.

--
Bye,

Daneel

Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:
> I understand your point regarding simplicity. I value simplicity. It is
> important, but I think there may be more important things. What do you
> think of the following:
>
> In a perfect world the rule on unaltered reprints would be taken loosely.
> The rule would exist, especially for the player's own good (not to
> accidentally confuse reprints with new cards, for which the rule is
> highly logical). Players who came to tournaments with unaltered
> reprints from a set that is not tournament legal yet would be tolerated
> without question, and noone would mind other players playing unaltered
> reprints, as they are the same cards they already know, even if they
> have a different expansion symbol.

Well, then it's not really much of a rule is it? It's more like the
reprint rule, but it's more annoying. Now, you have the situation that
someone could think, "Aw, no one will complain about that. . . " and then
they will be angry when they get called out on it. And yes, they'll get
angry, even if they're at fault.

> We don't, however, live in a perfect world. So when people show up with
> a KMW Blur or Blood Doll in their decks, some folks will actually
> complain about that. They will see to the judge having to find proxies
> for the reprinted cards. How does replacing a KMW Blur with a BH Blur
> actually make ANY difference? This seems to be beyond pointlessness.

They complain because there's a rule about that. And despite anything
else, players are generally going to make an effort to be tolerant about
that. The transcript of what happened wherever it did served to prove that
point. I was in a tournament where my predator tried to play Channel 10
and it wasn't legal. I pointed it out, and the local prince virtually
ripped the card from the offending person's deck and flung it across the
room. :) See, we handled it and it was fine.

But I could have made a point about it. And I would be correct in doing
so. I personally don't see a difference between a reprint and a new card,
because if someone says to me that cards of type X aren't legal, they
ain't legal. Now, I wouldn't be averse to allowing reprints, but
simplicity is to be valued above the case where folks don't follow rules.

Sounds like you're advocating changing the rules so that people would
follow them. In that case, I think that 30 pool is clearly not fair. It
unnecessarily hinders the newbie, since they don't know how to manage it
yet. I move that we increase the pool each Methuselah receives to 51. I'd
follow that rule.

> Of course, I see the general point of the rule, and I see the general
> point of keeping rules if they exist, but this particular example is
> just beyond me. Even if a rule is generally needed, and keeping rules
> is generally good, doing something stupid is still doing something
> stupid.

I don't think the rule is stupid. And you haven't shown me that.

> Aside, there's also the issue with new players needing the reprinted
> copies. I'm not sure about this, but I would think that the new players
> would especially value if they could use their freshly obtained cards.

That's *if* they show up with invalid cards. Which is potentially less
likely if you tell them that cards from set X aren't legal. Of course,
some people will associate with the DCI thought process, and so will find
this rule unintuitive. Doesn't mean that V:TES should conform though.

As far as the new players wanting to use their shiny cards. . . eh.
They'll always want to use their shiny new cards. Experienced players
would like to use them too -- all those esteems and undue influences and
berettas and suppressing fires. . . . What's the difference?

Simple. It's a goal.

Ankur

Messages.Author: x5m...@gmx.de
Messages.Body:
We have three possible solutions. What happens in a tournament in the
30 days.:

The existing rule. A player has a new Wake of Evening Freshness. Its
illegal. The player is pissed.

Reprints are allowed. A player has a Forced March, because he thinks it
is a reprinted crad. "There really was a Forced card, i am sure." Its
illegal. He is pissed.

All new cards and changes are legal immediately. A player has bulid a
deck around the old "Anarch Revolt", because he has no opportunity to
learn the new rule. His playing is illegal. He is pissed.

There is no solution, that can make all players happy, who dont look
exactly, whats legal and whats illegal in a torunament. In all the
cases, the existing solution is the simplest and clearest.
