Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:
>>> Please notice, there's two ways to look at an "inconsistency" here.
>>> You can focus on the expansion symbol on the card or you can look at
>>> whether the card's a reprint or a new card. You insist on suggesting
>>> the focus is on the expansion symbol is the natural thing, you're
>>> going to come to the conclusion that it's more complex to divide up
>>> whole sets into the legal and the illegal.
>>
>> Well, I'm "insisting" upon that based upon a series of arguments around
>> the fact that deciding whether something is a reprint or not is an
>> additional step -- a step which is not necessarily trivial for certain
>> (not-altogether-uncommon-or-pathological) cases.
>
> Insist on it for any reason you want, just notice that it's not the only
> way to view the situation, that other people "naturally" tend to view it
> otherwise, and that an argument which asserts that ITS way of seeing
> reality is the simplest one has a problem when real life evidence tends
> to suggest otherwise.

I'd say the same to you. I simply happen to think that the sort of new
player I'm talking about is more frequent than the sort you're talking
about. And I've given at least some basis for the fact that certain types
of new players (those who are excited) can cause a lot of unnecessary and
additional work for someone who's trying to promote them to play, because
they'll ask repeated "is this a reprint" questions. And no, as a promoter,
I won't feel like it's going to make a good impression to send them off
searching for websites if I've got the answer in my brain.

>> This basic point seems to be the point of our contention. Yes,
>> experienced players (and thus, most of those who post here) will tend
>> to think that it is far more natural and logical that reprints are
>> legal. But I'm allowing for those who wouldn't necessarily have been
>> posting here yet. . . you know, the new people.
>
> Of course new people. That's who I'm talking about, too. Who else would
> have shown up at the NE Qualifier with illegal decks?

Newer people than experienced, but veterans (perhaps) comparatively to the
folks I'm talking about. Two different mentalities.

> Sure. What makes you think it works any differently if you make the
> determination from a card's *name* rather than it's expansion symbol.
> Last I checked, the name was a visible attribute on a card, just like an
> expansion symbol.

Name in and of itself brings out other different sticky points, which
we're avoiding, remember? (Such as changed text of cards, new misprint,
etc.) I'm arguing these points from a less strong position than I could in
a strict sense, and it's still not an altogether unreasonable position.

>> Unless your observation includes a large demographic of players (read
>> new) that are not currently represented in this argument, you're bound
>> to come to a skewed conclusion.
>
> Fine - then let's make no assumptions about it either way - in which case,

Well, you couldn't really see the point I'm making but regardless. . .

> I don't want to here the argument that the existing system must be the
> simplest one. I'm simply pointing out to you that some don't see that way
> and here's evidence that maybe you're wrong - it's NOT the simplest way.

Ok, Fred. If we don't consider the definition of "simplest" from some
person or demographic perspective, this argument is meaningless. Your
point (at the start of the thread) was, and I'm paraphrasing here, "it's
much simpler to allow reprints as a scheme". No conditions, no other
caveats. I'm responding to that. It falls to me then to present to you
three things:

1) A counter-example
2) Reason to believe that the counter-example is not arbitrarily
constructed
3) Other consequences which may be as-of-yet unconsidered in said
counter-example

I've done these 3 things.

> That and the fact that the DCI uses the system and doesn't seem to have
> a problem with it.

The mentality of one game's players don't necessarily move to another's.
I'll freely admit that the later points I tried to make about Magic were,
well, dumb, but at least the previous sentence is correct. I could say any
number of extremely offensive statements about the stereotype of Magic
players, but let's not get into that. Let's just say, "they're different
folk".

> Gee, I had no clue this reason was so 'important'. Truth is, I'm just
> responding to your argument. Lest we lose perspective here, I don't
> think it's that important a rule either way, as I said at the onset.

Nor do I. But both of our arguments stem from considering certain types of
people, namely those who have basically just started playing. From *that*
perspective, taking a game that has a high learning curve and (at least
for some players, which I argue is a majority) adding complexity to it is
a bad thing.

> true. Clearly, that happens, and I fail to see what is so 'important'
> about requiring them to rework their decks at the last minute somehow
> (or worse, applying penalties to them if discovered during play).

Takes time, puts them on the spot, dunno really. On this I agree with you.
Not sure why it's a big deal. We seem like pretty nice folks all around.

>> There's that step we're talking about. The point where a player must
>> know more to execute the more logical rule that you're talking about. .
>> . . You know, I have players show up with invalid crypts for the first
>> few weeks/months they play the game. And though I tell them, I also
>> tell them that it's ok. It's because they simply *don't know*.
>
> All right, I don't see the communication glitch here but we're clearly
> talking past each other. If a player knows a previous version of the
> card is legal, he CAN use it. If he's never seen it before but knows
> the reprint rule, he won't TRY to use it - unless he takes the time to
> establish that it had been previously printed. I fail to see any
> problems with any of this.

K, Fred. Let's take the case of a player who's excited about playing this
game, as most new folks are. Now, how's he going to try to find out if
it's a reprint? Don't you think that his first line of attack is to ask
the person who taught him how to play? Seems like a simple question with a
simple answer, right? But then, when he/she says that this card is/isn't
legal, it might spark other questions of the same sort. That's one way.

Another is that he goes and looks online or at lists or whatever. This
takes time away in the early times from actual playing or deckbuilding. I
have argued that this is not optimal from the perspective of drawing a new
player.

Yet another is that he resigns himself to saying that he's never seen the
card, so it must be new, and therefore, he can't play it. I have *never*
had this personality of new player, ever. And I have a few under my belt.
This is the basic problem with your premise.

The above 3 paragraphs are one point. The second point is this: a
DCI-conditioned individual will associate more with the reprint rule than
the expansion symbol rule, and thus, consider it simpler. But even if
they conceptually recognize its simplicity as you've indicated above, in
practice, they'll end up doing more "work" as outlined above.

>> What if he's seen it before, but it's a promo card, which is also not
>> legal yet?
>
> Huh?!? That's scratching. If a new player doesn't know a promo card is
> not legal to play then he might play the promo card itself illegally -
> so this is not a new problem. Answer to this by either system: player
> must know the legal date to play all promo cards.

Nope, not scratching. My point is whether he'd play the version of the
card from the new set. In order to know, though, you're requiring him to
know more information, as we've talked about before. Remember, said new
player may not know or have realized that the card in question was
actually a promo card. He may not have the card either; just have seen it.

Echo comes to mind as a card that was released close to its set release.
Don't remember if she was legal when KMW was released, but I don't think
so.

>> What if he's seen it in someone else's box and isn't sure what set it
>> was from? What if he's seen it in a dream with pink bunnies telling him
>> that it's legal? Why not just have a one-stop check-it-here
>> check-it-now solution? I mean, seriously? What's the rush?
>
> Pretty much scratching on all of these. What if he sees a Return to
> Innocence or Madness of the Bard in another player's box and has no idea
> they're banned.

That's a good point. Thanks. The point here is that the what-ifs can cause
additional confusion and could lead to more illegal decks at tournaments.

>>> Unless you mean, players are going to look through all the precons and
>>> start wondering if they can use any of these cards before March 23rd.
>>> They can *ALREADY* do that! Only difference is that now, they'd have
>>> to look through the precon, go find out if the card already exists in
>>> a previous printing, AND have to go out and score an old version of a
>>> card. It's actually MORE complicated NOW.

I misunderstood your point here, and now I get it. This assumes that said
player decides he must play with card X which he doesn't have. We're (or
at least I'm) just talking about the actual process of knowing what's
legal or not, without going fishing for cards. That's a whole different
story that we can discuss some other time.

>> You're right. And I'm wondering how you're missing the point here.
>
> Well, maybe it's because it's not as good of a point as you think?

Ok, but I don't think you've indicated that to me.

>>>> Assuming they're going to do some checking, yes. But remember who
>>>> we're talking about: people who bring illegal decks to tournaments.
>>>> Now, how do you get these people to bring valid decks? Make things
>>>> simple.
>>>
>>> Let me ask you this: if this is all that complex, do you think the DCI
>>> is having problems with Magic? This isn't exactly an untried rule,
>>> you know. (My perception, for what it's worth, is no. They've never
>>> had much of a problem about it that I noticed.)
>>
>> Magic is a different animal. The players are different. The game is
>> simpler.

Eh, my arguments about Magic are dumb, as I said before.

> I don't quibble over any of this. Sure, it's a different. But it
> works. I think you're just scratching for points to evade just accepting
> that the reprints-allowed rule works fine. It doesn't cause a ton of
> problems like you're suggesting it might. I wish we could just agree on
> that rather than quibbling about an issue that to me, seems in way in
> doubt.

It works fine for those who already think in the DCI way. I never did, for
instance, because though I played Magic, I never played competitively. And
at least for the majority of my recruited players, it's the same story. No
competitive play. No knowledge of the reprint rule for Magic.

>> So, wouldn't that newbie feel like it's a bit unfair that he could have
>> used card X if he had just *known* it was legal?
>
> No, not really. Sorry (...again), this seems a bit silly, conjecturing
> 'resentment'. Most normal people just slap their foreheads and say,
> "HEY! I could have had a V8!" (Or a Dreams of the Sphinx...) If
> new-player- seething-resentment over cards they could have played but
> didn't know were legal, I'd advocate shooting them with tranquilizer
> guns. Aren't we already using them when new players discover an OLD
> card they'd never seen before and go berserk?

I don't really know what to say. I'm not constructing these examples out
of thin air. And with how many I've recruited, I at least have a
perception of having a good basis experience to make these points on.

>>> Agreed. It's the definition of "simple" that I maintain needs work.
>>> When real people tend to assume the opposite of the existing rule,
>>> that's a good indication that it's not as "simple" as it could be.
>>
>> Again, you're not lookinng at the people who might be confused by this
>> rule. You're only seeing experienced players.
>
> Again, no, I'm talking about new players. I don't know why you think
> I'm talking about experienced players. Experienced players know the
> rule either way and don't bring illegal decks to tournaments.

There are two sorts of new players. You're talking about one. I'm talking
about the other. My sort are actually probably newer players than
yours, but that in and of itself doesn't matter.

>> Right back at you Freddie boy. :)
>
> Check. :-)

Mate? Nah, then it would be over. :)

Ankur

> have argued that this is not optimal from the perspective of drawing a new

Sorry, to me, this also seems like stretching a point far past it's value.

so I don't think speculating on whether they do or do not wish to spend
time figuring out exactly which cards they can and can't use in a given
tournament is worthwhile. If they do, let them. If they don't, they
don't have to. Either way, trying to assert that this causes any kind of
REAL practical problem - on the order of players showing up at a tournament
with illegal decks they didn't know were illegal - is stretching reason
beyond the breaking point, IME. I guess YMMV but at least you understand
why I think reprints-allowed ought to be the rule.

That's another problem that comes up either way. *IF* he doesn't know
whether the promo card is legal or not, *THEN* he may just as well play
the original promo card illegally - as well as the possibility that he

>> is generally good, doing something stupid is still doing something
>> stupid.
>
> I don't think the rule is stupid. And you haven't shown me that.

I'm not saying the rule is stupid. Its enforcement is. That's what the
whole paragraph is about. In this particular case I see the reason not
to allow new cards (as in, newly designed cards, not reprints), and I
wouldn't want that changed. I also see a reason (albeit a weaker one)
to go with simplicity and simply state, no card of the new set is
tournament legal, regardless of whether it is a completely new card,
or an exact reprint of a Jyhad card. I also see the reason to keep a
rule once it exists. So, there are three very rational steps, but the
end product is still questionable.

I think that step one, having the 30-day rule for newly released cards,
is necessary.

Step two, that is, extending the 30-day rule to reprints, is a product
of simplicity.

Step three, abiding by the rules, is a logical part, as we are talking
about rules. Common practice could change that in practice, but then
again, there are people who would mind.

So it is step two (simplicity) versus an unintuitive result.

I'd go with changing step two (changing the rule to make an exception
for reprints). The next best thing is changing step three (abiding by
the rule), but that is harder and has a bit less of a point.

>> players
>> would especially value if they could use their freshly obtained cards.

Well, Blur has been around. You know the card. Facing a KMW or BH blur is
of no real consequence. Yet the system provides you with an option to be
a dick about something trivial. Not good.

>>> Insist on it for any reason you want, just notice that it's not the
>>> only way to view the situation, that other people "naturally" tend to

>>

>> player I'm talking about is more frequent than the sort you're talking
>> about.
>
> Sure. But I don't care because the existing rule cause problems; the
> reprints-allowed rule doesn't cause any real problems.

Um, not sure how you're getting this sort of umbrella-like conclusion. My
entire point is that it *does* cause problems, for a different group of
people.

>> And I've given at least some basis for the fact that certain types of
>> new players (those who are excited) can cause a lot of unnecessary and
>> additional work for someone who's trying to promote them to play,
>> because they'll ask repeated "is this a reprint" questions. And no, as

>> send them off searching for websites if I've got the answer in my
>> brain.
>
> This, to me, is just conjecturing a "problem" out of thin air. It's not
> really a problem. If you insist on regarding it as such, we'll just
> have to agree to disagree. But in my book, it's a really lame reason to
> oppose reprints.

The use of the phrase "insist" suggests that I'm forcing a point where
none exists. I'd urge you to experience the phenomena I'm talking about
before you suggest that it's manufactured for the purpose of argument.

>>> Sure. What makes you think it works any differently if you make the
>>> determination from a card's *name* rather than it's expansion symbol.
>>> Last I checked, the name was a visible attribute on a card, just like
>>> an expansion symbol.
>>
>> Name in and of itself brings out other different sticky points, which
>> we're avoiding, remember? (Such as changed text of cards, new misprint,
>> etc.) I'm arguing these points from a less strong position than I could
>> in a strict sense, and it's still not an altogether unreasonable
>> position.
>
> No, I don't remember. Every time they've been brought up, they turn out
> to be problems that already exist and are no more of a problem in this
> situation than they are in any other.

Well, I disagree, but I'm not going to introduce that complication into
this discussion at this time. We have enough to babble about.

>>> I don't want to here the argument that the existing system must be the
>>> simplest one. I'm simply pointing out to you that some don't see that
>>> way and here's evidence that maybe you're wrong - it's NOT the
>>> simplest way.
>>
>> Ok, Fred. If we don't consider the definition of "simplest" from some
>> person or demographic perspective, this argument is meaningless. Your
>> point (at the start of the thread) was, and I'm paraphrasing here,
>> "it's much simpler to allow reprints as a scheme". No conditions, no
>> other caveats. I'm responding to that.
>
> Well, you kind of have to take into account the sense of what I meant:
> that considering that people show up with illegal decks because they
> don't expect there to be a rule against new expansion cards that are
> reprints, it's just MUCH SIMPLER to allow said reprints. "Simpler" - as
> in, why are causing ourselves this problem when we don't have to. That
> doesn't exactly mean the reprints-allowed rule is conceptually simpler
> than the current one. It just means overall, the whole thing would be
> easier to deal with.

Sure, *once the scenario has played out poorly*, in other words, once
people have ignored the rules, we've got a problem. That's the case no
matter what the rule is. Yes, of course you'll have an easier time with
players not violating a more liberating rule. But then again, fewer people
will break (or try to break) NDA rules if we simply didn't have them. Does
that mean (by similar logic) that we shouldn't have them? What non-trivial
point are you making here?

My point is to the poor sap who wants to play the best deck possible, but
doesn't know what is and isn't going to help him achieve that. That is,
without research and/or asking those in the know.

>> The mentality of one game's players don't necessarily move to
>> another's. I'll freely admit that the later points I tried to make
>> about Magic were, well, dumb, but at least the previous sentence is
>> correct. I could say any number of extremely offensive statements about
>> the stereotype of Magic players, but let's not get into that. Let's
>> just say, "they're different folk".
>
> Fine. I just brought it up to demonstrate that it can work fine - to
> counter the impression some are suggesting that it cause problems to
> allow reprints.

I don't dispute that it can work fine. But I've again seen my scenario
even in Magic. It's tied to who learns what method first.

>>> Clearly, that happens, and I fail to see what is so 'important' about
>>> requiring them to rework their decks at the last minute somehow (or
>>> worse, applying penalties to them if discovered during play).
>>
>> Takes time, puts them on the spot, dunno really. On this I agree with
>> you. Not sure why it's a big deal. We seem like pretty nice folks all
>> around.
>
> Right. That's kind of where I'm coming from when I propose making this
> change.

If you're assuming that people break rules and will break rules, then I
suppose the more "freeing" rule is the better one. But I see frustration
and complication in the adhering-to-this-rule part by newer players. I
value simplicity for newer players (where we disagree on what's simple).
You value tournament expediency. It seems that we may simply have to
disagree about the impact of this rule.

>>> All right, I don't see the communication glitch here but we're clearly
>>> talking past each other. If a player knows a previous version of the
>>> card is legal, he CAN use it. If he's never seen it before but knows
>>> the reprint rule, he won't TRY to use it - unless he takes the time to
>>> establish that it had been previously printed. I fail to see any
>>> problems with any of this.
>>
>> K, Fred. Let's take the case of a player who's excited about playing
>> this game, as most new folks are. Now, how's he going to try to find
>> out if it's a reprint? Don't you think that his first line of attack is
>> to ask the person who taught him how to play? Seems like a simple
>> question with a simple answer, right? But then, when he/she says that
>> this card is/isn't legal, it might spark other questions of the same
>> sort. That's one way.
>
> Sure. To me, none of this seems like a bad thing. In fact, questions
> and interest are good things.

Absolutely. Questions and interest are good things. I'd rather them ask me
questions like, "Hey, how many masters should I play?" not questions like
"Hey, is Smoke Grenade a legal card?" I'd rather teach them the game than
explain to them what is and isn't legal for a 30-day period after which
all this "knowledge" which I've passed along is (relatively) meaningless.
I am excited to promote the game. But I want new players who can quickly
challenge active players, not those know know whether Taste was a reprint
or not.

>> Another is that he goes and looks online or at lists or whatever. This
>> takes time away in the early times from actual playing or deckbuilding.
>> I have argued that this is not optimal from the perspective of drawing
>> a new player.
>
> Sorry, to me, this also seems like stretching a point far past it's
> value. It a new player is that curious and wants to spend time doing
> that, I'm not going to tell him he's using his available time
> "incorrectly".

Nor would I. But *necessitating* it as a strategy doesn't seem at all
reasonable to me. Hey, some players are going to spend hours looking up
winning decks and strategies and learning each of the 1493 library cards
we've got right now. More power to them. But I'd like to say to someone
new "Just play. Don't worry about uber combos or reprints. Just play."

On another note, I don't find this a stretch. A new player generally makes
his decision to stay or leave within the first 2 months. The first month
is half his time. It's important what he feels he needs to do with it to
win.

>> Yet another is that he resigns himself to saying that he's never seen
>> the card, so it must be new, and therefore, he can't play it. I have
>> *never* had this personality of new player, ever. And I have a few
>> under my belt. This is the basic problem with your premise.
>
> Well, I don't think it's that much of a problem. There's lots of things
> you don't know as a new player, including a million cards you've never
> seen at all. And different players have lots of different
> personalities, so I don't think speculating on whether they do or do not
> wish to spend time figuring out exactly which cards they can and can't
> use in a given tournament is worthwhile. If they do, let them. If they

If it were speculating without some (limited) basis, I'd be more inclined
to agree. If we're talking about real practical problems, we need examples
and anecdotes and scenarios and case studies. You can't avoid that. I've
brought the weight of about, oh, 30 case studies. Maybe more.

> don't, they don't have to. Either way, trying to assert that this
> causes any kind of REAL practical problem - on the order of players
> showing up at a tournament with illegal decks they didn't know were
> illegal - is stretching reason beyond the breaking point, IME. I guess
> YMMV but at least you understand why I think reprints-allowed ought to
> be the rule.

I understand. You value tournament impact more than pre-tournament impact.
I value both, but tournament impact (once a violation has occurred, mind
you) doesn't affect me as much.

>>> Huh?!? That's scratching. If a new player doesn't know a promo card
>>> is not legal to play then he might play the promo card itself
>>> illegally - so this is not a new problem. Answer to this by either
>>> system: player must know the legal date to play all promo cards.
>>
>> Nope, not scratching. My point is whether he'd play the version of the
>> card from the new set. In order to know, though, you're requiring him
>> to know more information, as we've talked about before. Remember, said
>> new player may not know or have realized that the card in question was
>> actually a promo card. He may not have the card either; just have seen
>> it.
>
> I'm still confused. It doesn't matter which set he'd play the card from,
> the central problem is, he doesn't know the promo card is not yet legal.

He also doesn't know whether a card is a reprint. It's the same problem:
new player doesn't know old cards. He doesn't know how to distinguish
between them. He doesn't know what is and isn't legal. Also, this guy
could be malicious and simply use the excuse "but I thought it was a
reprint". NOW what would you do? There is no replacement for that card.

> That's another problem that comes up either way. *IF* he doesn't know
> whether the promo card is legal or not, *THEN* he may just as well play
> the original promo card illegally - as well as the possibility that he
> might play a reprint of the promo card. You haven't added a new problem
> that wasn't already there before, as far as I can see.

He may have, yes. I haven't added a new problem. The problem is: new
player does not know old cards. Many misunderstandings can take place.

> Agreed. And somehow, you haven't explained this in a way that makes me
> think so. I don't think there are any such what-ifs, but maybe I'm
> missing something or somehow not understanding a point you're trying to
> make.

I don't really know how to make my point any more clear or forcefully than
the above. We'll see how that works out.

Ankur

just what I stated - and not a new one introduced by reprints-allowed.

Maliciousness is another problem we can't solve with rules. I can only
say that this would be very rare. What would someone really have to gain
by this? The first competant player who knew the tournament rules would
call on it the instant the card was played and you can be pretty sure that
the resolution of that would in no way help the offender's game. He may
not get punished heavily for it (or even at all), but it's highly unlikely
pulling something like that on purpose would gain one anything in the long
run.

exacerbated. I see this sceneraio has rarer than hen's teeth - how
often does a promo card get released, reprinted, but 30 days hasn't
passed before reprinting? Even magazine promos that come out ahead of a
new expansion usually do so 30 days or more before the expansion is
released. So suffice it to say, this scenario doesn't bother me.

Fred
